chapters.title: Putting the bill back in
chapters.dek: Page 01's replication chapter left one line off the invoice. Adding it inverts the conclusion.

figures.title: The two forces, and their sum
figures.caption: Set costs to zero and the blue curve becomes monotone decreasing — page 01's world, where continuous hedging wins. Any positive cost creates the minimum. The practical reading: "how often should I hedge" has no answer until somebody states a cost and a risk aversion, and most disagreements about hedging frequency are really disagreements about λ.

checks.q: Your desk halves its commission rate. What happens to the optimal rehedge frequency?
checks.right: It rises. Cheaper trading moves the cost curve down, so the minimum shifts toward more frequent hedging and less residual risk
checks.why: It rises. The optimum sits where the marginal cost of one more rebalance equals the marginal risk it removes. Cheapen the marginal cost and you can afford to buy more risk reduction before it stops being worth it. Only at exactly zero cost does it run to infinity — which is page 01's continuous limit, and the reason that result is a theorem about a frictionless market rather than advice.

chapters.text: Page 01 sold an option, hedged it mechanically, and measured what was left. The answer was clean: the hedging error has a standard deviation that falls like 1/√N, so more rebalancing is monotonically better and the continuous limit is exact. That result is correct and it is also missing something, because every one of those N rebalances is an order that crosses a spread. Charge for them and two forces run in opposite directions. Hedging error still falls like 1/√N. But total turnover rises — each rebalance is smaller as N grows, yet there are more of them, and the sum grows toward √N. So the thing you are minimizing is a sum of a decreasing term and an increasing one, which is the classic shape of a problem with an interior answer. [equation: minimize E[cost] + λ · sd(P&L)] Reads as: trade off the money you know you will spend against the uncertainty you are trying to remove. λ is how much you dislike the uncertainty. At five basis points of cost and a moderate risk aversion, the objective bottoms out around 128 rehedges over a ninety-day option. Hedge less and the residual risk dominates; hedge more and you are paying spread to remove risk you had already mostly removed. The curve is genuinely U-shaped and the minimum moves with both sliders — raise costs and it slides left, raise risk aversion and it slides right. One honest note about the scaling. Cost approaches √N only asymptotically — between N = 128 and N = 512 the observed ratio is 1.76 against a predicted 2.0, because at low rebalance counts the initial hedge and the final unwind dominate the turnover and neither scales with N at all. The two forces, and their sum Distribution of total P&L at the chosen frequency Terms Set costs to zero and the blue curve becomes monotone decreasing — page 01's world, where continuous hedging wins. Any positive cost creates the minimum. The practical reading: "how often should I hedge" has no answer until somebody states a cost and a risk aversion, and most disagreements about hedging frequency are really disagreements about λ. Derivation — why the objective is U-shaped Split the total into the two things that move in opposite directions as you rehedge more often. [equation: hedging error sd ≈ c_1 / √N] Reads as: the risk you fail to remove falls like one over the square root of the number of hedges. This is page 01's replication result, unchanged. Now the bill. Each rehedge trades a smaller amount as N grows — the delta moves less over a shorter interval — but there are more of them. The expected absolute delta change over a step of length T/N scales like √(T/N), so total turnover scales like N·√(1/N) = √N. [equation: expected cost ≈ c_2 · k · √N] Reads as: the money you spend grows like the square root of how often you trade. Halving the interval does not double the bill, it multiplies it by about 1.41. Add them with a risk aversion λ and differentiate. One term falls like N^−1/2 and the other rises like N^1/2, so the sum has an interior minimum wherever their derivatives cancel. [equation: N* = c_1λ / c_2k] Reads as: hedge more often when risk aversion is high and less often when trading is expensive, and both effects enter one-for-one. Setting the derivatives equal, c_2k/2√N = λc_1/2N^3/2, and the powers of N collapse to a single N — so halving costs doubles the optimal frequency. The two-thirds power people sometimes quote belongs to a different cost model: a fixed ticket charge per rebalance makes cost grow like N rather than √N, and then halving the charge raises the optimum by only 59%. Which cost model your desk faces is a question about its fee schedule, not about options. Where it breaks. The √N cost scaling is asymptotic and the figure's own numbers say so: between N = 128 and N = 512 the observed ratio is 1.76 against a predicted 2.0, because at low rebalance counts the initial hedge and the final unwind dominate turnover and neither depends on N at all. The formula also assumes cost is proportional to size, which is the first thing that fails once your order is large relative to volume — at that point cost becomes convex in size and the optimum moves further left than this expression suggests. Try this Set the round-trip cost to zero. Predict what happens to the blue objective curve before you press it — does the minimum move left, move right, or stop existing?

chapters.title: Impact against timing risk
chapters.dek: Every parent order faces the same trade-off, and it has the same shape as chapter 01 for the same reason.

figures.title: Slicing an order: cost, risk, and the total
figures.caption: The same shape as chapter 01, arising for the same reason: a certain cost that grows with urgency against an uncertain one that grows with patience. Recognizing that these are one problem in two costumes is most of what execution theory has to offer.

figures.title: Work the order yourself
figures.caption: Buying everything at the open costs 60 basis points of impact every time. Spreading it evenly costs 1.9 on average over 400 days, but the result swings by 65.5 either way, because the stock moves while you wait; on the first day it drifts up all afternoon and the even schedule pays 93. A schedule that buys more early and less late lands between, at 4.8 with a swing of 47.3. There is no schedule that removes both costs. You choose which one to carry.

chapters.text: Having decided to buy fifty thousand shares, you face a second problem that is structurally identical to the first. Trade it all now and you pay a large, certain impact cost — you are the only buyer and you walk the book. Trade it over the day and impact falls, but the price wanders while you work, and where it ends up is uncertain . So it is cost against variance again: fast is expensive and predictable, slow is cheap and risky. The optimal trajectory is neither instant nor infinitely patient, and it depends on how much you dislike the uncertainty. The figure shows mean slippage and its standard deviation as the order is sliced more finely. Slippage falls quickly at first and then flattens, while the standard deviation keeps shrinking — but both curves are dominated at the fast end by impact and at the slow end by price risk. The impact coefficient is an assumption. Real impact models are fitted to proprietary execution data, the parameters differ by name, size and regime, and any number printed here would be invented. It is on a slider and labeled, and the honest use of this figure is to reason about which direction things move rather than to read a number off it. Slicing an order: cost, risk, and the total Order The same shape as chapter 01, arising for the same reason: a certain cost that grows with urgency against an uncertain one that grows with patience. Recognizing that these are one problem in two costumes is most of what execution theory has to offer. Now be the trader working the order. You need to buy 200,000 shares of a $50 stock today to finish a hedge, and the day is cut into eight slots that each trade about 250,000 shares. Buy a lot at once and you push the price up as you go; buy slowly and the price is free to wander away from you. Choose each slot's size and see the fills. Two shadow traders work the same day: one buys everything in the first slot, one buys an even eighth every slot. Work the order yourself This slot Buying everything at the open costs 60 basis points of impact every time. Spreading it evenly costs 1.9 on average over 400 days, but the result swings by 65.5 either way, because the stock moves while you wait; on the first day it drifts up all afternoon and the even schedule pays 93. A schedule that buys more early and less late lands between, at 4.8 with a swing of 47.3. There is no schedule that removes both costs. You choose which one to carry. Trader's lens An execution trader is scored against the arrival price, so every slice is a choice between a cost they can see (impact, now) and a cost they cannot (the price moving while they wait). How fast to trade depends on how much that second cost worries the desk: a hedge that must be done today is traded faster than an order with a week to run. Impact grows with your share of the volume; keep participation in the single digits when you can. Urgency means front-loading: pay a little more impact to carry less timing risk. The benchmark decides what "good" looks like; chapter 04 is that argument. Rule of thumb: impact here is 75 basis points times your share of a slot's volume; a quarter of the volume costs about 19. Try this Push the impact coefficient to its maximum and predict which way the optimal trajectory tilts — front-loaded, back-loaded, or flat — before you look.

chapters.title: The menu
chapters.dek: Each algorithm optimises something. Knowing which thing is the entire skill.

figures.caption: The recurring error is treating VWAP as a default. It is the correct choice when your objective genuinely is to be average, which is true for an index fund rebalancing and false for almost anyone hedging a position they have a view on.

chapters.text: Execution algorithms are not interchangeable and they are not ranked. Each is the solution to a stated objective, and picking one is choosing an objective, usually without saying so. Algorithm What it optimises When it is the wrong tool TWAP Even participation across time When volume is concentrated — you trade heavily when nobody is there VWAP Matching the volume-weighted average When you have alpha; it guarantees you trade late in a trend POV A fixed share of whatever trades When volume collapses, so does your fill rate — no completion guarantee Implementation shortfall Total cost against arrival price When the order is large relative to the day; it front-loads into impact Close / MOC Matching the official closing print Crowded, and a single auction is a single point of failure Liquidity-seeking Taking size when it appears Signals urgency; pays the spread by construction Pegged / midpoint Never crossing the spread Adverse selection — chapter 05 The recurring error is treating VWAP as a default. It is the correct choice when your objective genuinely is to be average, which is true for an index fund rebalancing and false for almost anyone hedging a position they have a view on.

chapters.title: The benchmark decides the verdict
chapters.dek: One execution, two reports, two conclusions. This is why execution arguments never resolve.

figures.title: Three schedules, two scorecards
figures.caption: Flip the trend to negative and the verdicts swap: patience now looks brilliant against arrival and unremarkable against VWAP. Nothing about the algorithms changed. The scorecard did.

checks.q: You are hedging a delta you want off the book today. Which benchmark should you be measured against?
checks.right: Arrival, because the risk began when the decision was made and delay is a real cost you are trying to measure
checks.why: Arrival. The reason you are trading is to remove a risk that exists from the moment you decided, so any drift between decision and completion is part of what the hedge cost you — and that is exactly what an arrival benchmark captures and a VWAP benchmark discards. Measuring a hedge against VWAP rewards spreading the order out, which is precisely the behavior that leaves you exposed for longer. The last answer is a joke with a serious edge to it: the benchmark should be fixed before the trade, because afterwards there is always one that flatters.

chapters.text: Take a single set of fills — a uniform execution, buying steadily into a rising market. Score it two ways. Against interval VWAP , it comes in at −0.00 . Dead on benchmark. The report says the algorithm did precisely what it was asked to do. Against arrival price , the same fills cost about 1.5 — the exact figure moves with the path, and it is reliably close to half the drift over the window , because a uniform execution buys at the average price and the average of a straight line is its midpoint. The report says the execution lost a point and a half against the price at which the decision was made. Both numbers are correct. They answer different questions. VWAP asks "did you trade better than the market's average during your window," which is a question about execution skill with the market's path taken as given. Arrival asks "what did the whole process cost relative to the moment you decided," which includes the market moving away from you while you worked. Neither is right in the abstract, and the choice is not innocent. VWAP forgives trend and punishes deviation; arrival punishes delay. A trader measured on VWAP is incentivised to spread out; the same trader measured on arrival is incentivised to hurry. Hand those two mandates to identical traders and you will get systematically different behavior and each will be optimising correctly. The practical rule: pick the benchmark that matches why you are trading. Hedging a delta you want gone is an arrival problem, because the risk started when you decided. Rebalancing an index is a VWAP problem, because being average is the objective. Three schedules, two scorecards The price path and where each schedule traded Market Flip the trend to negative and the verdicts swap: patience now looks brilliant against arrival and unremarkable against VWAP. Nothing about the algorithms changed. The scorecard did. Try this Set the trend to zero so the market drifts nowhere. Predict whether the two benchmarks still disagree, then turn the trend back up.

chapters.title: Dark venues and the fills you wish you had not got
chapters.dek: Resting at the midpoint saves the spread. The saving is not free, and what it costs is measurable.

figures.title: Where the price goes right after your passive fills
figures.caption: The distribution barely changes shape as informed flow rises — it shifts. That is what makes adverse selection hard to notice from a handful of fills and easy to measure from a few thousand: it is a small bias in the mean, not a visible change in the risk.

terms.Adverse selection: Getting filled precisely because the person on the other side knew something. It is not a fee — it is the systematic tendency of your fills to happen just before the price moves against you.

chapters.text: A dark pool matches without displaying quotes, typically at the midpoint. The appeal is obvious: no spread paid, no information leaked by showing an order. The problem is subtler and it is about who chooses to trade with you . When you rest passively, you do not decide when you get filled — your counterparty does. Uninformed flow crosses at random. Informed flow crosses when it is right , which is to say just before the price moves against you. So your fills are not a random sample of moments; they are selected toward the bad ones. The simulation makes the bias legible. With no informed flow, the average price move immediately after your fills is +0.00 — no bias, as it should be. Raise the informed share to 25% and the average post-fill move is −0.20 ; at 50% it is −0.40 . Both are simply the informed share times their 0.8 edge; the simulation lands within a few hundredths of that on any draw. You are not being unlucky. You are being selected. This is the mirror of the market-maker's problem: page 14 of this series looks at the same phenomenon from the quoting side, where the defense is widening. Here, resting passively, the defenses are different — minimum quantity constraints to avoid being pinged by small informed orders, venue selection based on measured post-fill drift, and simply accepting that a mid fill in size is sometimes a warning rather than a win. The number worth carrying: saving half a spread is not worth it if the post-fill drift exceeds half a spread , and whether it does is an empirical question about the venue, measurable from your own fills. Where the price goes right after your passive fills Is the spread saving worth the selection? Venue The distribution barely changes shape as informed flow rises — it shifts. That is what makes adverse selection hard to notice from a handful of fills and easy to measure from a few thousand: it is a small bias in the mean, not a visible change in the risk. chapters.title: Hedging with the basket
chapters.dek: An ETF is a wrapper whose price is held to its contents by an arbitrage with a cost. That cost is the whole story.

figures.title: Price against NAV, with the creation band
figures.caption: Widen the creation cost and watch tracking loosen — the price stops being held and starts drifting with demand. This single parameter separates an ETF you can hedge with from one you have to think about, and it is why the same wrapper behaves so differently across asset classes.

checks.q: An ETF shows thin volume on screen but its underlying basket is highly liquid. Can you hedge size in it?
checks.right: Usually yes. Liquidity is inherited from the basket, because an authorised participant can create shares against it
checks.why: Liquidity is inherited. A market maker quoting that ETF is not limited to the shares currently changing hands — they can take the other side and hedge in the basket, then create or redeem to square up. So the size you can do is set by the underlying, not by the ETF's own tape. The reverse is the trap worth remembering: an ETF with heavy screen volume on an illiquid basket looks tradeable and is not, because the arbitrage that would absorb your order is expensive to run.

terms.Authorised participant: A firm entitled to create and redeem ETF shares against the underlying basket. The arbitrage that holds an ETF near its NAV runs through them.

chapters.text: Hedging index or sector exposure with an ETF is usually cheaper than trading the basket, and understanding why requires understanding creation and redemption. An authorised participant can hand the fund a basket of the underlying shares and receive new ETF shares, or hand back ETF shares and receive the basket. That right is what pins the ETF price to its NAV. If the ETF trades above NAV, an AP buys the basket, creates shares, sells them, and pockets the difference — which pushes the premium back down. The mechanism is not free, so it does not pin exactly. It creates a band : the price can wander from NAV by up to the cost of doing a creation before the arbitrage becomes worth executing. Inside the band, nothing happens. At the edge, APs step in. Which gives the practical rule. When creation costs are low — a large liquid domestic equity ETF — the band is a couple of basis points and the ETF is effectively the basket. When creation costs are high — illiquid underlyings, different time zones, closed markets, credit instruments that do not trade — the band is wide, and the ETF's price is its own thing that happens to be related to NAV. Premiums and discounts in those products are not mispricings; they are the band doing its job. One more consequence worth knowing: ETF liquidity is inherited, not intrinsic . A thin-looking ETF on a liquid basket can absorb size, because an AP can always create against the underlying. A thick-looking ETF on an illiquid basket cannot. Screen liquidity is the wrong number to look at; the basket's liquidity is the right one. This single parameter separates an ETF you can hedge with from one you have to think about, and it is why the same wrapper behaves so differently across asset classes. chapters.title: Where it breaks
chapters.dek: Every number on this page rests on an impact model, and impact is the least observable quantity in the whole series.

checks.q: Your broker's transaction cost analysis shows your algo beating VWAP by three basis points every month for a year. What have you learned?
checks.right: Very little on its own. VWAP forgives trend and punishes deviation, so a strategy that trades passively in a drifting market beats it structurally — the arrival-price number is the one that would tell you something
checks.why: Very little on its own. Consistently beating a benchmark by a small margin is usually evidence about the benchmark rather than about the algorithm. The diagnostic is to score the same fills against arrival: if the two disagree persistently and in the same direction, you are measuring the interaction between your trading style and the benchmark's blind spot, not skill.

chapters.text: The U-curve, the optimal trajectory and the dark-venue simulation all share one input that nobody can measure directly. This chapter is about how much weight that input can carry. Impact models are fitted, not observed. You never see the price that would have prevailed had you not traded, so impact is inferred by comparing executions against a counterfactual that does not exist. Every estimate is therefore a model output conditioned on the sample of orders a firm happened to send, which is itself selected — you trade more when you think you can. The coefficient in this page's figures is a slider precisely because no honest version of it is a constant. Slippage attribution is contentious. Chapter 04 showed the same fills scoring on benchmark against interval VWAP and losing a point and a half against arrival. That is not a curiosity; it is the daily argument between a trading desk and the desk it trades for. Whoever picks the benchmark has picked the answer, and the choice is usually made by whichever side wrote the report. The close is crowded. A large share of daily volume prints in the closing auction, which makes it the cheapest place to trade and simultaneously the place where everyone else's order also is. Impact models calibrated on continuous trading understate what happens when a lot of correlated demand arrives in the same fifteen seconds, and the auction's price-formation mechanism is not the one the model assumes. Costs are not linear in size. The √N argument in chapter 01 assumed cost proportional to the amount traded. Beyond a few percent of daily volume that stops being true and cost becomes convex, which moves every optimum on this page to the left — hedge less often than the linear model says, because the marginal rebalance is more expensive than the average one. And the hedge itself is a choice. Chapter 06 hedged with an ETF, which introduces basis risk that none of the other figures price. A hedge that is cheap to execute and imperfectly correlated is not obviously better than one that is expensive and exact, and that trade-off is a portfolio question rather than an execution one. What survives all of this is the shape of the arguments rather than the levels. Costs create an interior optimum; trading faster buys certainty and pays impact; benchmarks encode a view; dark fills are adversely selected; ETF tracking loosens with creation cost. Those conclusions are robust to the parameters. The specific numbers are illustrations, and this page has tried to keep every one of them on a slider so you can see how much they move.

chapters.title: Check yourself

checks.q: Your desk halves its commissions. What happens to the optimal rehedge frequency?
checks.right: It roughly doubles. With costs proportional to size, turnover grows like √N and risk falls like 1/√N, so the optimum is linear in λ/k
checks.why: It roughly doubles. The optimum sits where marginal cost equals marginal risk reduction; with a √N bill and a 1/√N risk, those balance at N* = λc_1/c_2k, linear in cost. The 59% answer is right for a different desk — one paying a fixed charge per ticket, where the bill grows like N. And "roughly" is honest: the figure's turnover is only asymptotically √N, so the simulated optimum moves a little less than the formula says.

checks.q: At exactly zero trading cost, what is the optimal hedging frequency?
checks.right: Infinite — this is page 01's continuous limit, and it is the corner solution that any positive cost destroys
checks.why: Infinite. Page 01's theorem is exactly the zero-cost corner of this page's problem, which is why "hedge continuously" is a statement about a frictionless market rather than advice.

checks.q: Trading a large order faster does what to your risk?
checks.right: Reduces timing risk and increases certain impact cost — you are exchanging an uncertain loss for a known one
checks.why: You swap uncertainty for a bill. That trade is the whole content of execution scheduling, and where you want to sit on it depends on risk aversion exactly as in chapter 01.

checks.q: The same fills score on benchmark against interval VWAP and lose about a point and a half against arrival. Which report is right?
checks.right: Both are arithmetically right. They measure different things: VWAP forgives trend and punishes deviation, arrival punishes delay
checks.why: Both are right and they answer different questions. Pick the benchmark and you have picked the verdict, which is why the choice belongs in the mandate rather than in the report.

checks.q: Why are midpoint dark fills adversely selected?
checks.right: Because a resting midpoint order is most likely to be hit precisely when someone with better information wants the other side — the fills cluster before adverse moves
checks.why: You get filled when someone wants to trade with you. That is the same adverse-selection argument as page 14's market-making simulation, viewed from the other side of the quote.

checks.q: A thin-looking ETF sits on a highly liquid basket. Can you hedge size in it?
checks.right: Usually yes. Liquidity is inherited from the basket, because an authorised participant can create shares against it
checks.why: Liquidity is inherited, not intrinsic. The trap is the reverse case: heavy screen volume on an illiquid basket looks tradeable and is not, because the arbitrage that would absorb your order is expensive to run.
